raw_case_text:
A 16-day-old male presented to our emergency department with new-onset left facial nerve palsy for 1 day. Birth history significant for term vaginal delivery with vacuum assistance. There were no perinatal complications and he was healthy at birth (Figure 1). The mother had third trimester infectious screening completed about 1 month prior to delivery that was all negative. She had no known infections during pregnancy and no history of oral or genital lesions.
The day prior to presentation his mother noted the left side of his face did not move when he cried and he could not fully close his left eyelid (Figure 2). This was an abrupt change as he was previously moving both sides of his face normally. He was evaluated at a newborn visit at 5 days of age with no abnormalities. Other than the facial movement, he was acting appropriately for a newborn.
Initial examination was notable for an alert, vigorous, well-appearing infant. He had a normal-sized head, with head circumference z score of 0.04. Anterior fontanelle was open and flat. His pupils were reactive with normal bilateral light reflex. His cardiorespiratory, abdominal, and genital examinations were normal. His neurologic examination was notable for lack of movement of the forehead, cheek, and corner of the mouth on the left side when crying. Also notable for lack of tear production in the left eye. When blinking, it was notable that the left eyelid was not closing. All of this was consistent with a lower cranial nerve VII defect. All other cranial nerves were intact with normal neonatal reflexes and good strength for age.
In the emergency department, there was concern for infectious etiology, so a full neonatal sepsis workup was undertaken and unrevealing. Complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, coagulation studies, and urinalysis all were normal. The lumbar puncture was traumatic with >20 000 red blood cells, but otherwise normal. Given there was no concern for bacterial meningitis, he was started on acyclovir and admitted to the hospital.
Neurology and infectious disease teams were consulted. A brain magnetic resonance imaging and temporal bone magnetic resonance imaging were normal. Herpes simplex virus, varicella, and cytomegalovirus cerebrospinal fluid and blood polymerase chain reaction testing were all negative so acyclovir was discontinued. HIV and syphilis testing were also negative. Given negative infectious testing, oral prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/d was started on day of life 18 following discussion of risks and benefits with his mother. He demonstrated mild improvement in symptoms following 1 dose and was discharged with a total 7-day course of prednisone. The patient was lost to primary care follow-up for many months. During a discussion with his mother <2 weeks following discharge, his symptoms had resolved. He was seen in the emergency department for unrelated problems 27 days later and had no deficits on examination. At his 6-month well-child visit, he had no visible abnormalities and was growing well.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 16-day-old term male neonate presented with a 1-day history of acute-onset left facial nerve palsy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: After a normal newborn examination at 5 days of life, the infant's mother noticed on day 15 of life that the left side of his face did not move when crying and his left eyelid failed to close completely.
subjective.past_medical_history: Born at term via vacuum-assisted vaginal delivery without perinatal complications. Maternal third-trimester infectious screening (1 month prior to delivery) was completely negative, and the mother had no history of oral or genital lesions.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for acute left facial asymmetry and incomplete left eyelid closure with absent left tearing; vigorous feeding and normal neonatal behavior without fever or irritability.

objective.physical_examination: Alert, vigorous, well-appearing 16-day-old male with normal head circumference (z-score 0.04) and flat open anterior fontanelle. Neurological examination revealed a complete isolated left lower-motor-neuron cranial nerve VII palsy (absent left forehead, cheek, and oral commissure movement when crying, incomplete left eyelid closure on blinking, and absent left-eye lacrimation), with intact remaining cranial nerves, normal tone/strength, and normal cardiorespiratory, abdominal, and genital exams.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC, CMP, coagulation profile, and urinalysis were normal. Neonatal HIV and syphilis testing as well as blood HSV, VZV, and CMV PCRs were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Traumatic lumbar puncture (>20,000 RBCs) showed otherwise normal CSF parameters with negative CSF PCRs for HSV, VZV, and CMV. Brain MRI and dedicated temporal bone MRI were completely normal.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Diagnosed with idiopathic congenital/neonatal Bell's palsy (isolated left lower-motor-neuron facial nerve palsy; congenital syphilis, HIV, HSV, VZV, CMV, and structural brainstem/temporal bone lesions excluded). Empiric IV acyclovir was discontinued once viral PCRs returned negative, and on day of life 18 he was started on a 7-day course of oral prednisone (0.5 mg/kg/day), achieving complete resolution of the left facial nerve palsy within 2 weeks of discharge and normal development at 6-month follow-up.
